result: The authors reconstructed the evolutionary history of CID and NCBD domains through phylogenetic analysis, showing that NCBD is older than CID. NCBD was present in the protostome/deuterostome ancestor and can be traced in deuterostomes, protostomes, and cnidarians. CID appeared after the divergence of protostomes and deuterostomes (450-600 Mya) but was present in early deuterostomes before the first whole-genome duplication (1R). The CID/NCBD interaction emerged at the beginning of the deuterostome lineage around the Cambrian period.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C21-C26 are supported by phylogenetic reconstruction data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1-4. The phylogenetic trees and sequence alignments provide clear evidence for the evolutionary timing and distribution of these domains across species. The methodology using maximum likelihood reconstruction is appropriate and the conclusions about domain age and distribution are well-supported by the data.

result: The authors measured binding affinities between ancestral and extant CID/NCBD variants using ITC. The most ancient D/P NCBD formed a relatively weak complex with 1R CID (Kd ~5 µM), with all tested D/P NCBD variants yielding Kd values of 1.5-18 µM. By the time of the vertebrate-specific whole genome duplications (1R and 2R), the affinity had increased to ~200 nM, similar to present-day values, and was maintained in further speciation.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C6, C27-C30 are well-supported by ITC binding experiments reported in Figure 5, Table 1, and Figure 6. Multiple variants of D/P NCBD were tested to address uncertainty in ancestral sequence reconstruction, and all showed consistently low affinity (~1.5-18 µM). The increase in affinity to ~200 nM by 1R/2R and maintenance in extant species is clearly demonstrated. The experimental approach is rigorous with appropriate controls and replicates.

result: The authors characterized the structural properties of ancestral and extant CID and NCBD variants using CD spectroscopy. All tested CID variants displayed similar far-UV CD spectra typical of IDPs, with virtually identical overall α-helical propensity as measured by TFE titrations. CD spectra and thermal denaturations were similar for all NCBD variants, though the most ancient D/P NCBD variant was slightly less stable than subsequent variants.
evaluation: Claims C35, C36, C41, C42 are supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figures 5C-D, 7, and Tables 2-3. The TFE titration experiments show similar midpoints and curve shapes for CID variants, supporting the claim of identical overall helical propensity. The urea denaturation data for NCBD variants show similar profiles with a modest difference for D/P NCBD. The authors appropriately note the limitations in accuracy for free energy estimates due to broad transitions.

result: The authors used NMR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations with Metadynamic Metainference to characterize structural ensembles of three CID/NCBD complexes (ancient, 1R/2R, and extant). Evolution of higher affinity correlated with reduced conformational heterogeneity. The ancient complex was slightly less structured and more compact (helical fraction 0.41), the 1R/2R complex had helical fraction 0.44, and the extant complex had helical fraction 0.47. The ancient complex had more but less populated contacts than younger complexes.
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by NMR data (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Figure 9—source data 1) and molecular dynamics simulations using NMR chemical shifts as restraints (Figures 9-10). The NMR peak assignment was close to 100% for all complexes, providing high-quality restraints. The Metadynamic Metainference approach appropriately balances experimental data with force field information. The convergence analysis (Figure 13) supports the reliability of the simulations. The trends in helical content and contact populations are consistent across the evolutionary trajectory.

result: The authors conclude that new interactions involving intrinsically disordered proteins may evolve via a low-affinity complex which is optimized by modulating direct interactions and dynamics, while tolerating several potentially disruptive mutations. They demonstrate remarkably high tolerance to mutation in the interface of the CID/NCBD interaction in extant complexes.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C51-C53 represent the main conclusions of the study and are supported by the combined phylogenetic, biophysical (ITC, CD, NMR), and computational (MD simulations) data. The progression from low-affinity (~5 µM) to high-affinity (~200 nM) complexes, the similar affinities despite sequence variations across species (Table 1), and the structural analysis showing optimization through both direct contacts and reduced conformational heterogeneity all support these conclusions. The tolerance to mutation is demonstrated by similar affinities for variants with different residues at uncertain positions and across species.

result: The authors found that affinities between extant NCBD domains and human CID domains were surprisingly similar across several species (e.g., sea lamprey and human CREBBP NCBD have similar affinity for human NCOA3 CID). In contrast, affinities of p53TAD and PNT for ancient and extant NCBD were similar (~1 µM for PNT), suggesting these interactions were present before and preserved during evolution of the CID/NCBD interaction. The PNT domain is present in protostomes while CID is not.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33, C59-C61 are supported by ITC binding experiments in Table 1 and phylogenetic analysis. The similar affinities across species for CID/NCBD interactions demonstrate conservation of binding despite sequence divergence. The consistent affinities of p53TAD and PNT for ancient and extant NCBD variants suggest these interactions predated CID/NCBD and constrained NCBD evolution. The phylogenetic data showing PNT presence in protostomes but CID absence supports the evolutionary inference.

result: The authors tested reverse mutations in human CREBBP NCBD (A2106Q, Y2108Q, and A2106Q/Y2108Q) to probe the role of positions 2106 and 2108 in affinity evolution. The A2106Q mutation did not change affinity for NCOA2 CID, while Y2108Q and the double mutant resulted in slightly lower affinity (twofold).
evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by ITC data in Table 1 and Figure 12, but the authors note significant caveats: the mutations made NCBD less soluble, leading to precipitation and less reliable data with ill-defined native baselines. While the limited effect supports the computational predictions and demonstrates plasticity, the experimental quality issues prevent strong conclusions. The result is consistent with the overall narrative but cannot be considered definitively supported.

result: The authors analyzed amino acid substitution rates across domains in NCOA and CREBBP/p300. Substitution rates were higher for all domains during early animal evolution up to the fish/tetrapod ancestor (390 Mya). Within CREBBP, the substitution rate of NCBD was similar to ordered domains (HAT, RING/PHD), while KIX and TAZ1 were more conserved. The authors conclude that functional constraints rather than disorder per se determine substitution rates for CID and NCBD.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3. The methodology of counting substitutions and indels between ancestral nodes is appropriate. The finding that NCBD (disordered) has similar substitution rates to some ordered domains (HAT, RING/PHD) but different from others (KIX, TAZ1) supports the conclusion that functional constraints are more important than disorder status. The inference is reasonable and supported by citations to prior work (Brown et al.).

result: The authors used AGADIR software to predict that the stability of individual α-helices has changed during evolution. For example, α-helix 1 of CID from human NCOA1 and 2 displays higher α-helix propensity than α-helix 1 from human NCOA3 and ancestral versions.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are supported by AGADIR predictions shown in Figure 8. However, these are computational predictions rather than direct experimental measurements. The overall helical propensity measured by TFE titrations was similar across variants (C36), so the AGADIR predictions suggest local rather than global changes. The predictions are reasonable but represent a lower level of evidence than direct experimental measurements.

result: The authors analyzed how NCBD interacts with different ligands. NCBD employs distinct residues for interaction with IRF-3 (which adopts a completely different conformation) compared to CID and p53TAD. For CID and p53TAD, similar residues are used throughout evolution with different relative influences. NMR and folding experiments suggest NCBD can adopt two different conformations in absence of ligand.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by contact analysis from MD simulations (Figure 11) and citations to prior structural and NMR studies (Qin et al. 2005, Lee et al. 2010, Kjaergaard et al. 2010a, 2013, Dogan et al. 2016). The distinct binding modes are well-established in the literature. The contact analysis clearly shows different residues involved in IRF-3 binding versus CID/p53TAD binding. The claim about conformational heterogeneity (C65) is appropriately qualified as not experimentally confirmed for the IRF-3-bound conformation.

result: The authors analyzed structural differences between NCOA1 CID/NCBD and NCOA3 CID/NCBD complexes using available NMR structures. Only the first α-helix (Cα1) of NCOA1 and NCOA3 CID occupy similar positions, with Cα3 of NCOA1 aligning with Cα2 of NCOA3. The first α-helix of NCBD (Nα1) interacts with Cα1 in both complexes. Residues forming the Nα1/Cα1 interface are conserved in the deuterostome lineage, while Nα3 has accumulated five substitutions.
evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are supported by structural analysis of NMR structures shown in Figure 4 and sequence alignments in Figure 2. The structural superposition clearly shows the different arrangements of helices in the two complexes. The sequence conservation analysis is straightforward and well-supported by the alignments. These observations provide important context for understanding the evolution of the interaction.

result: The authors note that initial native contacts during binding between human NCOA3 CID and CREBBP NCBD are made between residues in the respective α1 helices of the two domains. Both Cα1 and Nα1 contain conserved leucine-rich motifs common in protein-protein interactions. Extant fruit fly NCBD has low affinity for human CID domains, and the leucine-rich motif in Cα1 is mutated in fruit fly NCBD.
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by citations to prior work (Iešmantavičius et al. 2014, Dogan et al. 2013, Kobe and Deisenhofer 1994), sequence alignments in Figure 2, and ITC data in Table 1. The conservation of leucine-rich motifs and their importance for the interaction is well-established. The low affinity of fruit fly NCBD for human CID and the mutation of the leucine-rich motif provide supporting evidence for the importance of these structural features.
